title: Lease epoch rebalancer and sticky-shard redelivery for low-latency async workers
creator: Sofia Martinez
description: Refactor async ingestion and worker coordination to introduce lease-epoch stamping and a sticky-shard redelivery path. Goal is to reduce transient duplicates, shorten failover recovery for shard moves, and exert smoother cooperative backpressure without increasing tail latency for hot tenants.
background: We currently observe repeated redelivery storms and long tail latencies during consumer rebalances or worker restarts. Existing retry logic is conservative (aggressive immediate reenqueue) which causes hot replays and head-of-line blocking. Several prior tickets touched similar areas (consumer backpressure, redis client upgrades), but we need a focused, incremental design that: 1) preserves per-shard ordering for clients that depend on it, 2) provides safe idempotent redelivery semantics, and 3) integrates with the token/credit-based flow controller used by intake gateways.
proposed_solution: Introduce a lease-epoch number attached to worker leases and message claims. When a worker claims a shard it stamps an epoch on in-memory processing records and on any temporary reenqueue entries. If a claim is lost, the rebalancer will only allow redelivery of messages from previous epochs into a ‘shadow replay queue’ for controlled, rate-limited consumption by the new owner. Add sticky-shard routing for messages with idempotency keys so duplicates preferentially route to the same shard for a short TTL. Implement cooperative backpressure: per-shard credit windows (configurable per-tenant), soft headroom thresholds that trigger delayed reenqueue into shadow queue rather than immediate visible push, and jittered drain to avoid thundering herd. Keep default behavior intact behind a feature flag for quick rollbacks.
tradeoffs: Pros: reduces duplicate processing and lowers failover-induced tail latency; smoother throughput under rebalances; preserves ordering for idempotent flows.
Cons: added complexity in lease coordination and shadow queue introduces operational surface area; requires changes to monitoring and runbooks; small latency overhead when stamping epoch metadata.
Decision: prefer gradual rollout with shadow queue TTLs tuned conservatively; we will measure before widening sticky-shard TTLs to avoid cross-tenant hotness.
Compatibility: Works with Redis Streams and Kafka-style partition consumers; Kafka integration will map partition offset claims to lease-epochs similarly to stream claim IDs.
acceptance_criteria: No user-visible increase in median latency for generation workloads in the canary tenants (<=+3ms).
Duplicate processing rate for rebalancing events reduced by >=70% compared to baseline during controlled failovers.
Shadow replay queue drains at controlled rate and never exceeds per-tenant inflight cap during test failure injections.
Feature flag allows fast rollback with zero-downtime for hosted API traffic.
Automated integration tests for lease-epoch handoff and shadow redelivery added to CI.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (dev): implement feature-flagged prototype and unit tests; land core lease-epoch stamping and shadow queue with default conservative config.
Phase 2 (canary): enable for 5 internal canary tenants, monitor duplication and tail latencies for 72h; iterate configs (ttl, replay-rate).
Phase 3 (staged): enable for low-traffic customer cohort and a subset of background jobs; run chaos tests (worker kill, network partition) against canary cluster.
Phase 4 (full): enable by default with backpressure defaults tuned; deprecate legacy immediate-reenqueue path in 4 weeks after stable metrics.
Rollback: flip feature flag off and switch consumers to immediate-reenqueue; run drain job to reconcile shadow queue.
testing_plan: Unit tests for lease-epoch invariants, shadow queue TTL enforcement, and idempotency-key routing.
Integration test: simulated rebalance with 50k messages, assert duplicates and tail latencies under thresholds.
Chaos test: worker process kill during mid-processing; verify new owner only receives shadowed items at controlled rate.
Load test: apply tenant-level burst traffic to validate credit window behavior and ensure no head-of-line blocking.
E2E test: route a representative customer workload through canary cluster and compare to baseline dashboards.
